new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (15 pp., 2-up, rotated 90, no text layer) and rendered PDF page 9 left half; it is printed p. 54, header 'A TENTATIVE PHONOLOGY OF ISIRAWA', section '4.1 Stress'. The page image reads exactly: 'There are three places in which stress may occur: ultimate, penultimate, or antipenultimate. Even though some words are differentiated by stress only: /'topa/ 'tree roots' akar kayu / /to'pa/ 'bow' anak mai / /'tore/ 'tree type' macam pohon / /to're/ 'name of a river' nama sungai / almost all non-verbal words and all the long form of verbs have penultimate stress. The few words with non-penultimate stress are names of places, kinship words, adopted words, and words that are possible historical…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per phonological word (1-7 syllables). Stress is lexically placed within a three-syllable right-edge window (final, penult, antepenult; never further left) and a handful of minimal pairs are distinguished by stress alone, but the overwhelming default is penultimate: almost all non-verbs and all long verb forms are penult-stressed, and words of more than three syllables are almost never non-penultimate. The exceptions are place names, kinship terms, loanwords and probable historical compounds.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only mentioned for the short form of the verb, which in clause-final position carries the phonological-phrase or sentence primary stress; 'Its secondary stress pattern is unpredictable' (p. 55). No secondary stress described for other words.
new_statements.exceptions: Minimal pairs /'topa/ 'tree roots' vs /to'pa/ 'bow', /'tore/ 'tree type' vs /to're/ river name; non-penultimate stress in place names, kinship words, adopted (loan) words and possible historical compounds; on some words stress fluctuates between speakers within a vowel cluster (p. 42); stress becomes very weak and almost disappears in rapid speech, and the non-phonemic vowel lengthening that accompanies stress disappears with it (p. 55). Tone is predictable from stress (§4.2: the stressed syllable always has high tone in non-verbs; long verb forms have a high-to-low glide on the stressed syllable).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 'The phonological word consists of a segment of one to seven syllables with one primary stress and is bounded by a short pause' (p. 54). Data from citation-form elicitation and limited text material (the authors call the analysis above the syllable preliminary). Clause-final short verb forms take phrase/sentence stress (p. 55).
new_statements.identity_note: Oguri & Erickson 1975 (p. 39) note minor dialect differences between villages east and west of Amsira; their analysis is based primarily on the eastern variety (Glottolog dialect Eastern Isirawa east1857), with fieldwork in a village using both. Language also called Saberi.
